title: System Health Checks
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of System Health Checks and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate system health checks.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces system health checks as part of scheduling, logs, and monitoring. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Find relevant system events, schedule jobs, build health checks, and choose useful metrics and alerts.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Monitoring should answer operational questions. Combine events, logs, measurements, and actionable thresholds rather than collecting data without a plan.

items.title: CPU and memory alerts
items.text: CPU and memory alerts: Start with a baseline, correlate the observation with the process or workload, and avoid inferring a bottleneck from a single metric.

items.title: Disk usage thresholds
items.text: Disk usage thresholds: Identify the relevant path or storage layer first, inspect its current state, and make changes only in a disposable lab with a recovery plan.

items.title: Service availability
items.text: Service availability: A backup or rollback is useful only when its integrity and restoration procedure have been verified in a separate test location.

items.title: Failed system units
items.text: Failed system units: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.title: Defining meaningful health criteria
items.text: Defining meaningful health criteria: Include timestamps and enough context to connect the event to a service or process; choose a threshold that leads to a concrete action.

content_blocks.execution_mode: manual-terminal; requires a local Linux environment or disposable VM; no isolated Linux runner is provided by CodeLeaf
content_blocks.expected_output: Failed service/unit summary on a systemd host.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: System Health Checks. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume system health checks behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: This is an inspection command. Formatting, partitioning, and repair commands can destroy data. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Monitoring should answer operational questions. Combine events, logs, measurements, and actionable thresholds rather than collecting data without a plan. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate system health checks. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Monitoring should answer operational questions. Combine events, logs, measurements, and actionable thresholds rather than collecting data without a plan.
Use evidence rather than assumptions; make platform differences explicit.
Protect credentials and data, and plan how to reverse state-changing operations.
